title: Mekies offers update on Hadjar's injury recovery
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has missed the three races since the summer break ended, sitting out Zandvoort, Monza and Madrid as he recovers from an injury sustained in training. The Frenchman hurt his wrist in the three-week break, and has been on the sidelines ever since.

In his absence, Liam Lawson has stepped up into the vacant Red Bull seat, with Yuki Tsunoda filling Lawson’s cockpit at Racing Bulls.

Those two have done an admirable job in difficult circumstances, but they face a wait to see just who will be where for the next Grand Prix in Azerbaijan.

Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies clarified the situation in the wake of the Spanish Grand Prix, confirming that there had been no additional setbacks for Hadjar, and that his recovery was taking as long as expected.

“Isack is good... There is nothing wrong with Isack's recovery. I think we have learned that it's fundamentally normal time for the sort of injuries he has,” Mekies said.

“So, we will continue with the same approach than what we had, we will evaluate the situations in a weeks’ time, we have a full week, with more than a full week to evaluate the situation to see how he feels.

“And then to put him on the simulator, to expose him to real-life constraints… If he feels close to 100%, we go for it. If he feels the recovery is not completed, we will stick [with] our approach to put his recovery first.

“What we don't want to do is by having an early return, compromise his long-term capacity to come back to 100%.”

Hadjar has made a strong start to his time with Red Bull, with eight top-10 finishes, including a podium in Monaco. He has also managed to out-qualify Max Verstappen three times.

This injury setback is far from ideal, with the Frenchman having missed out not just on points, but on learning more about the RB22 as everyone continues to get to grips with the new generation of cars.

He has still attended races and thus will have been looking at the data, but that is not the same as driving and understanding exactly where the latest upgrades are taking the car.

In his absence, Verstappen has taken two podiums to show what the car is capable of, while Lawson has finished in the points twice from his three drives with the team.

Another driver in recent memory to come back from a wrist injury was Lance Stroll, who had a bicycle accident prior to the start of the season in 2023. He missed testing but drove in the opening race and scored points despite having a broken wrist and toe.

Daniel Ricciardo was out considerably longer than Stroll when he broke a bone in his hand in 2023 after crashing in practice at Zandvoort. The Australian wound up missing five Grands Prix – with Lawson being his replacement at the time.

It seems that Red Bull are happy to leave it late to make a call on whether Hadjar will return to the cockpit for the upcoming triple header, or whether he will remain on the sidelines for the time being.

title: 'Bit of a shock to the system' leading Cadillac – Budkowski
excerpt:
Marcin Budkowski admits that returning to Formula 1 has been "a bit of a shock to the system", having been put in charge of the Cadillac team.

The Pole has been with the American team for nearly a month, having replaced Graeme Lowdon as Team Principal just before the Dutch Grand Prix at the end of August.

Budkowski is no stranger to F1, having worked with multiple championship-winning Formula 1 teams across sporting and technical divisions and within senior leadership teams, including Prost, McLaren, Alpine and the FIA.

Having left the sport in 2022, Budkowski found himself in a new role with media organisations Eleven Sports Poland and Viaplay, before the call from Cadillac.

Ahead of last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, Budkowski admitted that the return to a prominent role in the sport had been a bit of a shock.

"What hits you first is the pace of F1, which I knew well but a few years out of the sport and it's a bit of a shock to the system because it's incredibly fast-paced, technical and hard-working, especially when you start in a new team and new project," said Budkowski during Friday's teams' press conference.

"The other thing is the first time I sat again on the pit wall in FP1 in Zandvoort and I had 12 channels blasting in my ears. It took me a little bit of time for my brain to get used to it.

"But the reality is, if you bring it back to the essentials and basics, it's about people, it's about building the team. It's about putting the right people in the right positions, getting everybody to work together and in terms of leadership, give them a vision and align everybody in that direction. That hasn't changed."

Cadillac have endured a difficult maiden season in F1 so far, remaining the only team on the grid yet to score a point, with Valtteri Bottas' P13 in the Chinese Grand Prix the team's best result to date.

Despite the lack of pace and reliability so far, Budkowski has been encouraged by what he has seen, despite having been at the helm for only three races.

"I've seen a lot of good things in the team, and it's pretty impressive given the time they had to build the team and conditions with the entry and everything.

"A lot of good things, there's no legacy compared to some other teams. There's a lot of open-minded, constructive discussions going on but there's also a number of shortcuts that are being taken, which is inevitable when you build a new team in such a time.

"It's about working in some areas that need more attention. In the short-term, reliability. We've seen we've struggled with that in some areas and just getting the operational excellence to the next level, which is not the level of a top team as of today, but that's understandable.

"Longer term, there's some clearer priorities emerging for what we need to do and better, mostly to improve our performance and our pace."

title: Tsunoda reveals his biggest mistake at Red Bull in 2025
excerpt:
Yuki Tsunoda has enjoyed a surprise three race cameo in 2026, slotting into Racing Bulls in place of Liam Lawson following Isack Hadjar’s injury. While it remains unknown whether Tsunoda will get a fourth outing this season, the Japanese racer has certainly made the most of his unexpected comeback.

Tsunoda is Red Bull’s reserve driver this season, having lost his race seat at the end of last year. After being promoted to Red Bull from the third round of the 2025 season, Tsunoda struggled to make much of an impact and was resigned to playing a support role in Max Verstappen’s championship bid.

Speaking on the latest episode of official F1 podcast Beyond the Grid, Tsunoda explained just how tough 2025 was for him, after many years of relative success at Racing Bulls under their various guises, and exactly what he felt was his biggest mistake.

“One thing about myself I think, if I say [being] completely honest, I have a big enough ego to not change my driving style,” Tsunoda said. “I know what I'm doing in terms of driving. I believe in myself, so I never try to change my driving style to other drivers, even though the driver is competitive and fast.

“Obviously Max, it's a different case, he's a World Champion, he proves a lot of things and I still learn a lot of things from his driving. [It was] probably the first year out of any years since I started that I thought about changing driving style and tried to do something similar to Max.

“But in my perspective, if I just look at data, I didn't really see a huge difference in terms of driving. What I think now is the biggest mistake in last year was to try to replicate the set-up what he's doing.”

Tsunoda scored just seven times out of the 21 Grands Prix he contested with Red Bull, in a car that Verstappen took to second in the championship. The comparison between the two late in that season was stark, with Verstappen winning five of the final eight races, while Tsunoda in the same period recorded a P6, P7 and P10 finish.

That resulted in Tsunoda losing his seat, with Hadjar promoted from Racing Bulls to replace him.

“When I got told, I still remember, I didn't feel that much of huge disappointment or devastated feeling. Obviously, still disappointed and pretty sad that I'm not driving next year. But not as I expected, I don't know why.

“I fought really hard. I fought more than ever in that 2025 year, more than ever. And even if I look back now, I don't have much regret. I gave everything and the outcome is something I didn't like, obviously, but honestly, I just gave everything.”

Tsunoda believes the struggles he went through in 2025 have made him a better driver, and he has impressed for Racing Bulls.

In a new generation of cars, which are very different from what he drove last year, Tsunoda has done well in the three races he has contested – especially in Zandvoort, where the Sprint format meant he only had one practice session to get used to all the changes.

The issue Red Bull are still trying to correct on the RB22

“Going back to this Netherlands story, jumping into the car that I’ve never driven, Sprint Qualifying format, team is doing really well, you know, running P5 in Championship, [knowing] that you can't really mess up for the race, you want to have points,” he added.

“Somehow, I was like really, [feeling] okay. I didn't feel anything, that much, of pressure.”

Tsunoda finished 11th in Zandvoort, one place ahead of his team mate. But he thenfinished 10th at Monza to pick up a point for the team and help them in their fight against Alpine.

“The feeling I had, crossing the line, finishing P10, is definitely a bit more special P10 than certainly last three years of my career. Felt like really similar feeling towards first time I scored points in AlphaTauri [in my] first year.

“I felt very valuable, [more] than usual. I was so happy, team are happy, and the kind of moments that you can celebrate with the team – that we had a good race weekend – is something I didn't have for a while. It was a very nice moment.”

As to Tsunoda’s future, he is still trying to secure a full-time drive for next season. But it is a tough ask, with very few open seats left available.

“My primary focus is F1. I'm trying to be back. That's my target and I'm not thinking anything else. For myself, it's fortunate that I got opportunities so I try and maximise it and hope I can be back in 2027.”

title: The power unit manufacturers with the most wins in F1 history
excerpt:
Ferrari may be the most iconic team in F1 history, with their scarlet liveries and roster of legendary drivers, but Mercedes drew alongside them at the top of the list of the most successful power unit manufacturers with Kimi Antonelli's win at the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix.

From these two motorsport powerhouses to defunct companies like Coventry Climax and BRM, here are the top 10 engine producers with the most Formula 1 wins over the last 76 years…

=1. Ferrari – 251 wins

Ferrari were part of the inaugural F1 season back in 1950 and haven’t missed a year since, enjoying vast success over the decades with drivers like Alberto Ascari, Niki Lauda and Michael Schumacher.

They’ve also managed to net a colossal 251 victories with their own engines in that time – Charles Leclerc celebrated the team’s 250th at the 2026 British Grand Prix, while the extra one came from Sebastian Vettel’s maiden win with Toro Rosso in 2008, when they were a customer of the Scuderia.

Taking it back even further, Ferrari’s very first Grand Prix triumph was thanks to Jose Froilan Gonzalez, otherwise known as the Pampas Bull. He joined the team for five rounds in 1951 and finished on the podium at every one, including taking the win at Silverstone.

=1. Mercedes – 251 wins

Mercedes only competed in two F1 campaigns (1954 and 1955) before taking a hefty sabbatical, returning in part as an engine supplier for Sauber and McLaren in the mid-1990s, with Brawn GP and Racing Point joining their customer list at a later date.

Their original stint produced two Drivers’ Championships for Juan Manuel Fangio, but their modern power unit achievements are largely down to McLaren’s Mika Hakkinen (1998 and 1999 World Champion), Brawn GP’s Jenson Button (2009 World Champion), and of course, Mercedes’ full re-entry to the sport in 2010.

Why Brawn GP’s fairy tale is the F1 story that keeps on giving

Although they came back to the sport as a constructor with Schumacher and Nico Rosberg, it took two years to win a race, and another two before they clinched their first title.

By that time, Lewis Hamilton had signed for the squad and went on to claim 85 of Mercedes’ total wins while Rosberg, Kimi Antonelli, Valtteri Bottas and George Russell have also contributed to the record.

3. Ford Cosworth – 176 wins

The Cosworth DFV was one of the most dominant engines ever seen in F1, delivering 155 wins across outfits like Team Lotus, Brabham, Tyrrell and Williams. If a squad didn’t make their own engine between the 1960s and 1980s, this was the one they were all desperate to use.

Jim Clark secured its first win at the 1967 Dutch Grand Prix, where he drove from P8 to P1 in the Lotus 49, but a greater indicator of its success was the fact that every single race in the 1969 and 1973 seasons was won by a DFV-powered car.

The shift into the turbo era forced Ford Cosworth to evolve, with later variants of the engine clinching an additional 21 wins. These were predominantly achieved by Benetton and McLaren, but Giancarlo Fisichella holds the honour of netting the final victory at the 2003 Brazilian Grand Prix with Jordan.

4. Renault – 169 wins

You can’t speak of turbocharged engines without mentioning Renault. They were the first to regularly use the invention, and after two seasons of agonisingly poor reliability – it took 14 races to log their first finish – 1979 produced the breakthrough they needed.

Jean-Pierre Jabouille, who had patiently endured every retirement to that point, won that year’s French Grand Prix, but it was Alain Prost’s arrival in 1981 that unlocked Renault’s potential. After three years and nine triumphs, they declined as a works team once he departed, leading to their eventual withdrawal in 1986.

Alonso’s first F1 title win with Renault remembered

Ironically, they accomplished more when turbocharged engines were banned in 1989, when they began to supply Williams. Further collaborations with Benetton and Red Bull increased their number of wins to 169 overall, with Esteban Ocon taking their final one at the 2021 Hungarian Grand Prix.

Renault once again departed F1 at the end of the 2025 season, leading Alpine to switch from the French manufacturer to Mercedes under the new-for-2026 regulations.

5. Honda – 89 wins

Like Renault, Honda have had a somewhat fractured presence in F1, with their first entry occurring in 1964. They found early success by building their own engine and chassis as Richie Ginter reached the top step at the 1965 Mexican Grand Prix.

The company’s focus moved to road cars before they came back as a supplier for Spirit, Williams, Lotus, McLaren and Tyrrell at various times between 1983 and 1992. Not every team received the same level of factory support, but Nigel Mansell, Nelson Piquet, Ayrton Senna and Prost all proved that Honda could provide an unbeatable engine.

However, they pulled out again due to financial reasons before eventually purchasing BAR, which became Brawn GP when Honda suddenly exited again amid the 2008 economic crisis. Finally, they enjoyed a fruitful partnership with Red Bull from 2019 onwards, and Max Verstappen gave them their first win in the V6 turbo-hybrid era.

Their total ultimately reached 89 victories over four separate stints, with the 2021 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix marking their last, but that was far from the end of Honda’s time in F1 – more on that later.

6. Coventry Climax – 40 wins

Coventry Climax had manufactured engines since the turn of the 20th century, but it wasn’t until the 1950s that they began to appear in racing cars. Although Stirling Moss scored their first win at the 1958 Argentine Grand Prix, it was clear that their standard 2-litre engine wasn’t powerful enough to regularly compete with their rivals.

Things changed in 1959, when a 2.5-litre version took Jack Brabham to World Championship glory. The engine was also valuable in Lotus, Cooper, Brabham, and Lola chassis as it won 40 Grands Prix between 1958 and 1965.

It bowed out in style as Clark secured the 1965 title with his third and final career Grand Slam at the German Grand Prix, with Coventry Climax leaving the motorsport world when the 3-litre formula was introduced.

Five current drivers compared to past F1 stars

7. Honda RBPT – 38 wins

Verstappen’s hard-fought 2021 drivers’ title also marked Honda’s departure from F1, but they continued to help his team transition to their own in-house engine production named Red Bull Powertrains (RBPT).

As such, a new agreement was signed that saw the team take over the Honda engine IP to the end of the 2025 season, with the company providing support when required. This led to one of the most dominant years of recent memory as Red Bull won all bar one race in 2023, with the team scoring 860 points.

2024 and 2025 weren’t quite as productive, but they nevertheless ended with 38 victories overall to take seventh on the list.

8. TAG Porsche – 25 wins

Short-lived but immensely successful, this engine was used by McLaren between 1983 and 1987. Built by Porsche and funded by TAG, it was originally planned to debut in 1984, but Lauda insisted that they should test it beforehand and so the car was modified to accommodate the engine for the Dutch Grand Prix.

It was effective almost immediately and Prost made the most of it to win the season-opening 1984 Brazilian Grand Prix, though it was his team mate Lauda who would be crowned that season’s champion.

Between them, they netted 25 victories with the engine before McLaren changed their allegiance to Honda in 1988, inspired by the strong performances the Japanese company had logged with Williams.

9. BMW – 20 wins

The early years of F1 featured on-and-off private entries with BMW backing, but it was in the 1980s when the German manufacturer fully committed to the sport, deciding to directly challenge Renault’s turbo engines with their own version.

While they initially negotiated an exclusive deal with Brabham, the team opted to rely on Cosworth-powered cars, straining the fledgling relationship. Team Principal Bernie Ecclestone was convinced to give them a chance that paid off at the 1982 Canadian Grand Prix, won by Piquet.

More triumphs followed, but the ban on turbocharged engines for 1989 brought a temporary end to BMW’s involvement. They went on to take Renault’s place in a deal with Williams and delivered a competitive engine for the 2000 season, with a more aggressive evolution securing victory at the 2001 San Marino Grand Prix.

By 2003, Williams could consistently fight for wins but weren’t able to match Schumacher’s dominance with Ferrari, resulting in the end of the partnership in 2005.

BMW’s subsequent purchase of Sauber was a less successful venture – they only claimed one win, with Robert Kubica at the 2008 Canadian Grand Prix, and decided to sell the team back to Peter Sauber.

10. BRM – 18 wins

British Racing Motors, also known as BRM, got off to a shaky start in F1 as their overly ambitious engines didn’t generate the results they were hoping for. However, after some delayed development, Jo Bonnier claimed their first win at the 1959 Dutch Grand Prix to provide a much-needed boost.

Alfred Owen, a partner in the company, threatened to cancel the entire project if they didn’t start to achieve more, and chose to promote former Rolls-Royce employee Tony Rudd to the role of Chief Development Engineer. This proved to be a stroke of genius as he fixed basic problems that had plagued the team for years, culminating in Graham Hill’s triumph in the 1962 Drivers’ Championship.

BRM also began to sell engines to privateers, but their performances turned lacklustre and they left F1 in 1977 with 18 Grand Prix victories – 17 as a works team, and one under Team Lotus.

title: Alpine announce Mike Elliott as Chief Technical Officer
excerpt:
Alpine have announced that Mike Elliott is joining the team as Chief Technical Officer, marking his return to Formula 1 after leaving Mercedes towards the end of the 2023 season.

Elliott brings a wealth of experience to the position, having worked in the sport across 23 years since first becoming an aerodynamicist for McLaren back in 2000.

He went on to progress to other roles within the team before moving to Renault in 2008, remaining with the Enstone-based outfit until 2012 when he joined Mercedes.

After taking on the position of Head of Aerodynamics, the Briton would later become Technology Director from 2017 to 2021 and then Technical Director between 2021 and 2023.

He subsequently swapped roles with James Allison in 2023 to become Chief Technical Officer, before his departure was announced six months later.

In a statement confirming his appointment at Alpine, the team stated that Elliott will “oversee the technical and engineering functions at the team's factory at Enstone” in his new position, adding: “He has a proven track record in the sport, having contributed to an impressive eight Constructors' and eight Drivers' Championships.

“Elliott's arrival at Enstone strengthens the team's technical capabilities as the team looks to build on the improved performances on track and close the gap to the top four teams.”

title: Danielsson confirmed as Wild Card for F1 ACADEMY Austin round
excerpt:
F1 ACADEMY has announced that Alexia Danielsson will represent TeamViewer, the series’ Official Partner, as the Wild Card entry for Round 5 of the 2026 season in Austin.

The Swedish racer started racing single-seaters in 2022, moving up from Aquilia Formula 1000 to Nordic 4 two years later and scoring her first victory in the series last season. Additionally, she won on debut in the Porsche Sprint Challenge Scandinavia in 2025, before delivering a points-scoring rookie season in the F4 CEZ Championship this year.

Danielsson was one of the standout performers in last week’s F1 ACADEMY Rookie Test in Navarra, claiming the second-fastest time overall.

The 17-year-old will make her debut behind the wheel of the #45 TeamViewer operated by Hitech car, which will feature a special edition livery showcasing the role of communities in supporting women’s career progression – on and off the track.

Celebrating TeamViewer’s Forward Together campaign, which highlights how being part of formal and informal communities helps women enter and advance in sports and tech roles, the design includes 250 inspiring women.

Those featured represent communities focused on leadership development, advancing women in technology, empowering the next generation in STEM, strengthening professional networks, and driving greater inclusion in motorsport and automotive industries.

"It has been an absolutely incredible few days," said Danielsson. "First, to be given this opportunity by McLaren and then to perform so well at the F1 ACADEMY test was more than I had dared hope for.

"And now it is also official that I will race as a Wild Card in F1 ACADEMY during the United States Grand Prix, which feels absolutely amazing. Racing at COTA in front of such a huge crowd, right in the middle of a Formula 1 weekend, will be an experience I will never forget and something I can build on going forward."

Danielsson spoke further of her excitement at driving during F1's visit to Austin, adding: "More than anything, I’m just really excited to get the chance to race during a Formula 1 weekend. I’ve only been to an F1 race once before, and that was at Zandvoort in the Netherlands a month ago, when McLaren announced me as one of their drivers for the Rookie Test.

"My main goal for the weekend is to learn as much as I possibly can. I’m also competing for a place on the grid for the full season next year, so if I get that opportunity, I want to be as prepared as I can be."

Karin Fink, Head of Commercial Operations, F1 ACADEMY said: “Motorsports has always had a strong community behind it, and this is no different at F1 ACADEMY. The drivers are supported by so many around them, so it is nice to see some of those communities that inspire change for women, both on and off the track, featured on TeamViewer’s livery. By creating spaces where women not only belong but also have the opportunity to engage and share knowledge, we are able to empower more women to advance, no matter the industry.”

Faith Wheller, VP of Brand and Sports Partnerships, TeamViewer added: “Building on our campaign last year where we brought visibility to role models, this year we wanted to do something just as important to helping women advance. Forward Together highlights the need for communities and the role they play in our careers.

“The opportunity to support a young talent like Alexia in her F1 ACADEMY debut while also featuring many women who have supported the next generation in other industries is why this livery is so important. We look forward to being in Austin this October to support Alexia in person.”

title: How Verstappen won the ‘biggest race’ of his motorsport career
excerpt:
Just a few days after recording a podium finish in the Spanish Grand Prix, Max Verstappen was at another track and on the hunt for another trophy – the four-time F1 World Champion taking part in Red Bull’s special ‘Max vs 100’ karting event.

Held at Silverstone on Wednesday evening, the challenge was clear: overtake and eliminate 100 competitors – including Red Bull athletes, content creators and more – from the very back of the grid in 30 laps (or 75 minutes).

Red Bull, who have a long track record of stunts across various sports, described it as “the world’s biggest go-kart race”, with the action being broadcast live on Disney+, covered extensively across social media and treated like a headline encounter.

After a couple of practice days for an enthusiastic field of challengers, overseen by Racing Bulls driver Arvid Lindblad, things became serious when Verstappen arrived to get his first taste of a 2.5km track that blended Silverstone’s kart venue and sections of its F1 layout.

Verstappen’s pace – displayed to devastating effect in F1 over the last decade – was obviously never in question, but would the Dutchman have the time, space and dash of fortune required to pull off an ambitious charge from 101st to first?

“It’s a long way! A very long way!” Verstappen smiled during a pre-race interview as he walked from the front to the back of the grid – the size of the challenge appearing to dawn on him moments before the 1800 start.

What followed was box office entertainment.

Verstappen’s P101 to P1 charge

Shuffling forward in his kart to gain momentum as soon as the lights went out, Verstappen had ducked and dived past a gaggle of rivals by Turn 1, where he somehow managed to avoid being taken out in the bottleneck, and then strategically took to the grass to avoid various spinners.

His rapid rise continued through the rest of Sector 1 and Sector 2, until Race Control threw a Full Course Yellow to cover off further incidents.

It felt like Verstappen had managed to pick off 20 or 30 karts amid the drama. At a push, 40 or 50. Yet incredibly, when the timing screens updated, he found himself in 37th position, having made up a whopping 64 places in just one tour.

“Not a bad first lap, then!” Verstappen chimed on the radio when informed about his progress.

After the racing resumed, Verstappen climbed to 25th by Lap 4, 10th by Lap 6, and fifth by Lap 7, the number of karts out on track dropping and dropping until just three others remained: those of F1 journalist Jacky Martens, YouTuber Zac Alsop and Red Bull Ford Powertrains technician Lewis Osler.

The front three, led by polesitter Martens, joked over the radio about how they might work together to form a roadblock when Verstappen arrived, but in reality, there was no stopping the F1 superstar.

After just 35 minutes, and 14 laps, Verstappen had caught and passed them all.

“That was simply lovely,” Verstappen chuckled over the radio once he had eliminated the final kart, adding that “it’s my first win of the year, so I’ll take this one!”

Speaking to select media, including F1.com, afterwards, Verstappen reflected: “I grew up racing a lot in karts, then because of your formula career you don’t really get a lot of time racing them anymore, so it’s always nice to go back and have a go at it.

“I got three or four laps on the track, and that was basically my practice. Before that, it’s always very hard to know what to expect, so it’s also better then not to overthink the situation, and just feel it once you sit in the kart. But I think the most that I’ve been on a track with is like 40 karts, maybe, so a hundred is a lot!”

Verstappen’s fastest lap of the race was 2m 20.673s, with the next best being a 2m 23.327s from Martens, some 2.6s slower.

“I knew my lap times when I did the prep laps, and I knew the Qualifying lap times of the others, so I knew that it was possible [to win], but it also really depended on my first two laps,” said Verstappen. “They went better than expected, so that of course helped a lot.

“Before the race, I said, ‘Let’s be bold and say that I will pass 40 people in Lap 1’, and then they told me [what it was] at the end. It was a good effort. Some people got really excited on the new [extended] part of the track, and there was a bit of a road blockage going on, but I managed to swerve around it, and it worked out well.

“When the lights go out, you kind of just see where the gaps are, and then you also kind of need to trust a few people around you, that they don’t do anything crazy. To be honest, they didn’t. They were very excited with each other, but they were actually quite nice to me! They weren’t crashing into me or whatever.”

“He sees something we don’t see”

Track Designer and Race Director David Terrien was one of many onlookers at Silverstone who could only smile at what unfolded, with Verstappen’s aggressive approach, differing lines and later braking points visible from the outset.

“Going through the traffic of such a big field, no one has done it,” Terrien commented. “There’s never been a karting race with so many karts. So, even Max was questioning himself just before the start, how he could go through the traffic.

“When you look at the replay, he picked the right spots. Every time there was a gap, he went for it. He was on the right side of the track when there was a crash going on the other side. I think that’s what makes the difference with Max – his starts, and his reaction time. He showed his skills in all aspects.

“I was talking to Max’s race engineer and we were looking at the replay of the start. He sees something we don’t see. He sees a gap that’s going to open, and it’s not open yet. So, I think that’s a race vision. That’s something he has that most of the drivers don’t have.”

For Verstappen, as well as that element of competition, having joked about there being “no mercy” whenever his helmet goes on, Wednesday’s event was another Red Bull exercise that he will keep in mind for a long time – having previously driven an F1 car down a mountain and raced caravans with Daniel Ricciardo.

“Sometimes I get reminded of what I actually did in the past, and I’m like, ‘Oh my God, did I really do that?’” Verstappen said. “It’s definitely one of the best ones out there. I mean, how many times do you have the opportunity to create something like this? Racing against a hundred other people from other disciplines or sports.

“I think it’s great that with Red Bull, they always come up with some crazy, fun things, and it suits me as well. I think also the way that it was organised today… I know it requires a lot of effort to be able to do something like this, and it’s a lot of fun to be a part of that.”

So, could this become a tradition?

“That’s what I said! I was like, ‘Maybe 200’, and then we’ll see again,” Verstappen responded, before signing off from the press conference and enjoying what will go down as one of his most memorable victories.

title: What's new with the F1 Sprint in 2027?
excerpt:
The 2027 Formula 1 calendar is out and, among other things, you will have noticed there are more Sprints than ever before. Here's what you need to know...

How many more Sprints are we talking and why are we increasing?

The Sprint has been a hit and so due to the increasing popularity of the format, there'll be four more than in 2026, bringing the overall total to 10.

Since the Sprint concept was introduced in 2021, data shows that total viewership of Sprint weekends is 12% higher than non-Sprint weekends.

Sprint Qualifying is up to three times more popular with fans than practice (Sprint Qualifying replaces second practice on a Friday afternoon on non-Sprint weekends).

Meanwhile, 82% of attendees at Sprint weekends say it adds value to their ticket with competitive sessions taking place on three days, rather than two on a traditional weekend.

Data also shows 75% of F1 fans believe Sprint events add greater value to a season’s calendar.

As a result, the number of Sprints has risen from three each year in 2021 and 2022 to six each year between 2023 and 2026 with 10 planned for next season.

Gotcha. Will any venues get a Sprint for the first time?

Yes – Bahrain, which hosts the season opener, Australia, Japan, Monaco plus the season finale in Abu Dhabi will all get their first taste of the Sprint format.

Sorry, did you say Monaco is getting a Sprint?

Yep, you read that right. One of the most exhilarating sessions to watch in Formula 1 is Qualifying in Monaco as drivers navigate the tight and twisty streets of Monte Carlo.

Now, fans will get to enjoy not one but two of those spectacular sessions in the Principality.

Sprint Qualifying will take place on Friday ahead of the Sprint on Saturday morning (which replaces FP3) and then Qualifying for the main Grand Prix takes place later on Saturday.

Formula 1 reveals calendar for 2027 season with 10 Sprint events

Okay, so you've mentioned five of the Sprints – what about the other five?

Canada will host a Sprint for the second successive year, with Mercedes duo George Russell and Kimi Antonelli having delivered a sensational battle for the lead there earlier this year.

Silverstone gets its third Sprint after hosting one in 2021 and earlier this year, while Monza gets its second Sprint, six years after the Temple of Speed hosted its first.

Brazil extends its record of having hosted the most Sprints as it returns for the sixth edition at the iconic Interlagos track in Sao Paulo.

Qatar is back with a Sprint too, with Lusail getting a fourth one in five years.

With Abu Dhabi also hosting one, the season will end with back-to-back Sprints, leaving more points available for the final two Grands Prix weekends of the year.

At the other end of the calendar, with Bahrain, Australia and Japan hosting their first Sprints, it sees the season start with three Sprints in the first four race weekends – and that will reward teams who are fast and competitive straight out of the box.

Great stuff. Just remind me about the format of a Sprint?

Of course! As the name suggests, it's a short race. It runs over 100km, which is around one-third of a typical Grand Prix distance. It lasts roughly 30 minutes.

There are no mandatory pit stops like the Grand Prix and, while they are not banned, given the Sprint is so short it's not worth boxing for fresh rubber.

Points are awarded for the top eight positions with eight for the winner down to one for P8.

The introduction of the Sprint means the number of practice sessions are reduced from three one-hour sessions to just one 60-minute run.

Sprint Qualifying is a shortened version of the main Qualifying session, with SQ1 running for 12 minutes, SQ2 for 10 minutes and SQ3 for just eight minutes.

All in all, it means more competitive sessions across a season.

title: Australian GP addresses possibility of hosting 2027 F1 season-opener
excerpt:
Australian Grand Prix organisers have confirmed that the Melbourne race will not substitute in as a potential 2027 season-opener if it cannot be held in Bahrain.

In the 2027 calendar which was published on Wednesday, Albert Park was pencilled in as the third round of the season across April 1st-4th, after the season begins with a double-header in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia on March 12th-19th and 19th-21st, respectively.

However, owing to the uncertainty in the Middle East prompted by the ongoing Iran War, there remains the possibility that the season does not start in Sakhir and Jeddah, with Melbourne, which hosted the opening race between 1996 and 2019, and again in 2025 and 2026, a potential replacement.

This would mean moving the race forward three weeks to mid-March, and Australia and China jumping forwards in an effective swap with Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, but for a number of reasons, this is not feasible.

One is that between March 11-15th, covering that weekend, Australia are hosting England in a special one-off 150th anniversary Test at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG), located within walking distance of Albert Park.

Another, is that the pit-building at Albert Park has been demolished and is in the process of being rebuilt, and will be fully operational for the 2028 race, with partial facilities available for 2027.

"Our date’s been locked in now, April 1-4, and clearly we’ve got a big asset being built behind us that has some timelines attached to it,” Australian GP Corporation CEO Travis Auld told Australian media.

"So we’re pretty much locked in at that April 1-4 date, and I think it would be difficult for us to move that date now.

"Our contract with F1 has us as being somewhere between race one and three each year.

"We’ve had race one the last two years. I think what’s worked really well for us has been a race early in the season. The story of the season is still taking shape.

"And so this year it will be race three."

The article continues below.

Australia to host its first Sprint race

When the 2027 calendar was announced, Albert Park was confirmed as one of the 10 hosts of a Sprint race, and will follow Bahrain, Japan, Monaco, and Abu Dhabi in hosting one for the first time.

It is something Auld revealed the organisers had lobbied aggressively for.

"I know we had lengthy conversations about our desire to have a sprint race," he continued.

"I think they’re awarding a sprint race to us is a sign they trust us as an event. But importantly, they trust us as a city to put on great events.

"The stats say it brings more value to the event from a viewership point of view.

"I think the numbers say 10-12% increase in viewership. Fans enjoy the sprint qualifying three times more than they do enjoy free practice. And so from a fan point of view, it’s certainly way more compelling."

title: Breaking: Formula E bombshell as Penske team acquired
excerpt:
Fortescue Zero is set to become the first Australian-owned team on the Formula E grid, after agreeing to take over the Penske Autosport operation for the 2026/27 season.

The mining giant's electrification arm has acquired the Penske Formula E team and will run it as a customer outfit using Jaguar's Gen4 powertrain, subject to approval from the FIA and Formula E's promoter, FEO.

The move will take Jaguar's presence on the grid to six cars in total, once Fortescue Zero's two entries are added to the four already fielded by the factory Jaguar squad and Envision.

Fortescue Zero already has a long-standing relationship with Jaguar as a technical partner, and has been involved with Formula E since the championship's early seasons, supplying technology including as the official Pit Boost provider for the past two campaigns.

The company's motorsport roots trace back to Williams Advanced Engineering, before it developed into an engineering business specialising in high-performance electrification, technology it now applies to commercial electric vehicles and heavy industry.

Penske confident Fortescue will move Formula E team forwards

Fortescue Growth and Energy CEO Gus Pichot said the switch from technology supplier to race team marks a natural progression for the company.

"For more than a decade Fortescue Zero has been the brains behind some of the groundbreaking technologies powering and transforming electric racing," said Pichot. "Now, we're going to show the world how we can compete on the track as well.

"Progressing from the pit lane to the grid is the next chapter in our motorsports story. We're here to race, to win and to innovate.

"At Fortescue, it's in our DNA to go to the extreme, push the limits and go further and faster than our competitors. For us, motorsports is more than just a chance to take home a championship trophy, it's a platform to develop, test and home in on the next great technologies that will transform industries beyond racing."

Fortescue Zero Electromobility chief technology officer Travis Hester said the switch to running a full team gives the company's engineers a new proving ground.

"Formula E is pushing electric racing to another level, creating completely new engineering challenge," he said. "That is exactly where we want to be, at the front of the grid, solving difficult problems and finding the next competitive advantage.

"Motor racing allows Fortescue Zero engineers to design & develop technologies at the cutting edge of performance and efficiency. Battery, software and hardware technology is proven in the harsh environment of racing, then efficiency applications applied throughout Fortescue's mining and energy portfolio, as well as Fortescue Zero's automotive and defence customers."

Penske Autosport owner Jay Penske said he is confident the team he built will thrive under its new ownership.

"We are proud of what we have built with this team and the people who have competed at the highest levels of elite racing."

"Fortescue Zero has a clear ambition for electric technology and motorsport and we know it will build upon the great foundations we have laid and lead to future success."

Formula E CEO Jeff Dodds welcomed the arrival of a long-time partner as a fully-fledged competitor, saying: "Fortescue Zero has been a vital technology partner for Formula E from day one, standing alongside us since the inception of the Championship."

"Formula E is far more than a race series, it's an incubator for peak performance and ground-breaking technology, and Fortescue Zero exemplifies both. We are excited to see the competitive edge and innovation they will bring to the GEN4 era of the ABB FIA Formula E World Championship."

title: Sergio Perez opens up on new Cadillac development: 'Never seen anything like it'
excerpt:
Both Sergio Perez and Cadillac team-mate Valtteri Bottas were left highly impressed.

Sergio Perez has described Cadillac's new Silverstone factory as the most impressive facility he has encountered in his Formula 1 career.

Perez toured the facility alongside team-mate Valtteri Bottas last week ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix at the new Madring circuit. The two drivers held technical meetings with engineers and staff working on the car project.

Cadillac's operational base at Silverstone sits alongside the team's under-construction headquarters in Fishers, Indiana, and powertrain facilities in North Carolina, forming the backbone of the American manufacturer's multi-hub infrastructure.

Perez did not hold back on his assessment of what he saw. Speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, he said: "We were at the factory, and it's very impressive. I've never seen a factory like this in my career. It's really, really impressive.

"It was really nice to see it. We had talks with the engineers, with all the people involved in the project, the plans and stuff. It was nice to catch up with everyone."

Asked what made the new base stand out, former Red Bull driver Perez pointed to the freshness of the operation from top to bottom.

"First of all, it's because everything is new: the equipment they have, the platforms, how nicely it is connected, all the different departments," he said. "It's like a new home, very well organised. It was really good to see."

Perez's comments echo those of team principal Marcin Budkowski, who used the Silverstone facility to push back on suggestions that the team's British base is merely a stopgap before operations shift entirely to the United States.

Budkowski said the visit from Bottas and Perez had left a strong impression on both drivers, and framed the factory as proof that talk of an imminent relocation is wide of the mark.

"We just opened a new factory in Silverstone," he said, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "Anybody who has doubts that this is a temporary facility should come and visit because it's quite impressive.

"We had Valtteri and Checo come in and have some technical meetings there and speak to the staff, and they were really impressed. So was I on the first day I walked in.

"We are effectively building some facilities in the US as well. We will progressively develop a footprint in the US, whether that's through manufacturing capability or others.

title: Ollie Millroy relives Shanghai fireball: 'We both ended up crying'
excerpt:
The moment Ollie Millroy found himself trapped in a burning Ferrari after a severe crash, Loek Hartog didn’t hesitate for a second. The Dutchman stopped his Porsche, grabbed a fire extinguisher, and pulled his fellow driver from the wreckage. In an interview with RacingNews365, Millroy speaks in detail about the crash, the rescue, and the impact the incident has had on him.

Ollie Millroy has revealed details of his horror crash that left his Ferrari 296 GT3 engulfed in flames at the Shanghai International Circuit at the weekend, and fearing for his life before the intervention of fellow racer Loek Hartog, who was able to haul him from the wreckage.

The incident happened on Saturday, September 5, during a Chinese GT Championship race at the hairpin turn in Shanghai.

Two Ferraris collided at high speed after making contact with a BMW. One of the Ferrari 296 GT3s, driven by Millroy, burst into flames.

Millroy was unable to free himself from the car. Hartog, driving a Porsche, pulled up alongside the wreckage without hesitation, ran to marshals to grab a fire extinguisher, and dragged Millroy clear of the burning car.

Millroy was taken to hospital, where doctors found he had suffered five broken ribs, a broken collarbone, a broken hand and finger, and a bruised lung.

Speaking in an in-depth interview with RacingNews365, Millroy reflected on the crash and Hartog's actions.

"It's a strange feeling, you know?" said Millroy.

"Something I've never experienced before and that I think most people will never experience at all, being that close to life-altering injuries, severe burns, or even death.

"On the one hand, you feel incredibly lucky, but on the other hand... When I watched the accident again, you could also say I was incredibly unlucky, because there was absolutely nothing I could do about it.

"Yeah, it really is a very strange feeling. And to be honest, I don't think I'll really be able to process my emotions until I'm back home and see my kids."

Coincidence or fate?

Millroy said he was conscious throughout the ordeal, but has no memory of the 30 seconds before the crash or the hour that followed. It was only when Hartog visited him in hospital that the full picture emerged.

"The first time I heard that Loek had pulled me out of the car was when he came to see me at the hospital that evening," said Millroy.

"He started telling me about it and then showed me some videos and things like that. The two of us were sitting there, and we both ended up crying. It was incredibly emotional, because up until that moment, I really had no idea what had happened."

The crash has forged a close bond between the two drivers, to the point that a group chat has been set up including Hartog's parents. Millroy said he has come to see the timing of Hartog's presence behind him that day as almost fated.

"This moment has, as it were, been inside him since birth," said Millroy. "It's just in his nature. Of course, he's an incredible driver and incredibly competitive, but this is truly in his DNA. To be honest, I feel like he was destined to find himself in that position at that moment.

"You really get that feeling when you talk to his whole family. They're all such wonderful people. I was just incredibly lucky with the timing and the situation, and that he happened to be driving behind me during the race."

Wake-up call

Millroy hopes the crash will serve as a wider lesson for the motorsport world.

"I want this to be a wake-up call for all authorities, circuits, and staff involved," he said. "For every marshal who stands somewhere along the track at, say, Brands Hatch every weekend and thinks, 'Actually, it's been a while since I took my fire safety course. I think I'll sign up for that again.'"

He added that he and Hartog intend to "do everything possible" to ensure "more lives can be saved" in similar situations.

"That's where I see the real beauty of this story: in what we can achieve in the future and how we can use this situation we've both experienced to improve safety. There simply can be no excuse for this.

"There are 32 GT cars worth between one and one and a half million dollars racing around the Shanghai circuit. There's an enormous amount of money in that paddock and in that championship.

"Money should be completely disregarded these days when it comes to safety in motorsports, especially at this level.

"But really, that applies to every level. So we want to make sure this story actually leads to changes and that it opens people's eyes."

title: GPDA chief counters Madrid F1 track criticism
excerpt:
Alex Wurz, the head of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, has weighed in on the critcism that was directed towards the Madring last weekend.

The all-new circuit built in Madrid became the new host of the Spanish Grand Prix this year.

However, it failed to produce an exciting race, with minimal wheel-to-wheel action throughout the 57-lap grand prix - a feature that was also present in the junior categories.

It led to some criticism from several drivers, but Wurz insisted that creating a new track in a street setting has major constraints.

“Track design is not as simple as just drawing a few lines on an A3, A4 [sheet] or on a CAD programme,” Wurz told the Sky F1 podcast.

“You need to consider topographics, soil issues, plot boundaries, fire safety rules of a country. You need to run a business, meaning you need to place spectators and all the marshals, etc.

“You need to understand crowd flow, dimensioning of all those items. Infrastructure above, beside, below the track, constructability, budget constraints.

“There is an enormous list which is restricting.

“You mentioned half of the circuit is in the exhibition centre, and I think that was utilised to what it could be.

“We can't ask the promoter to relocate individual exhibition holes, that would be too much. So those 90-degree corners, maybe they're not to our best taste, but we can respect some of those.”

[Article continues below]

Wurz hopes for Madrid improvements

The Madring is on the F1 schedule for the long-term, signing a 10-year deal with the sport.

But following an underwhelming first edition, Wurz insisted there are elements to the layout that can be improved.

“Where I think things could have been done or could also in the future be optimised, is on the property on the other side of the highway, which was land.

“There wasn't anything there, so you looked at something which, at least at 50 per cent of the circuit, had no real topographical constraints.

“Maybe for us, unknown constraints of civil engineering nature and topography - but the topography actually is really cool.

“They made perfect use of it with Turn 12, the banked corner. Some other aspects, I think there is where the big wins can happen for the future.”

title: Formula E issues defiant statement as question mark hangs over F1
excerpt:
Formula E is still intent on starting its new season in Saudi Arabia this December, despite other championships continuing to move events away from the region.

Formula E has issued a defiant statement surrounding its scheduled season-opener in Saudi Arabia, following the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

The all-electric championship's new season and Gen4 regulatory cycle are set to get underway at the Jeddah Corniche Circuit from December 17th to 19th; however, other categories have actively moved events away from Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing conflict.

F1 cancelled its race in Jeddah earlier this year in April, while the FIA and World Rally Championship announced on Thursday afternoon that they had moved their finale from Saudi Arabia to Italy.

While F1 opted against racing in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain earlier this year – Malaysia will host the Bahrain Grand Prix next month – it remains to be confirmed whether its final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will take place.

In addition, F1 announced on Wednesday that its 2027 season will start in the Middle East, with a question mark already being raised as to whether it will be possible.

In recent weeks, Saudi Arabia has become more involved in the conflict, with a region just 300 kilometres from Jeddah having recently been targeted by missiles from the Houthi rebels. The nation has also used ballistic missiles itself.

Despite this and other championships moving events away from Saudi Arabia, Formula E remains fully intent on starting its new season in the country.

Formula E still intent on Saudi Arabia season start

A decision on whether the Jeddah E-Prix can take place does not need to be made until closer to the middle of November, when pre-season testing takes place in Madrid.

One Formula E team informed RacingNews365 that it does not need significant notice regarding Jeddah, as it will simply be a case of freight heading there after Madrid or, instead, to Mexico City, which will host the second round.

Preparation is already ongoing in Jeddah for Formula E, with the championship monitoring the situation closely.

In a statement issued to RacingNews365, Formula E co-founder and chief championship officer Alberto Longo said: "We are looking forward to opening the 2026/27 ABB FIA Formula E World Championship in Jeddah this December and launching the revolutionary Gen4 era.

"As with all our international events, we continuously monitor the situation on the ground alongside local promoter partners, authorities, and international security experts.

"The safety and security of everyone involved in the championship is always our top priority. Preparations for the season opener at the Jeddah Corniche Circuit are ongoing, and we will update all stakeholders should there be any developments."

How much longer will F1 take to make a call on its races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi?

The FIA has opted to cancel Rally Saudi Arabia as the closing round of this year's World Rally Championship, seemingly intensifying the pressure on F1 to reconsider its own end-of-season visits to the Middle East.

The FIA and WRC Promoter have confirmed that Rally Saudi Arabia, originally scheduled for November 12-15, will not form part of the 2026 WRC season.

The governing body said it had worked "extensively" in recent months with the Saudi Automobile and Motorcycle Federation (SAMF), the local organising team and championship stakeholders to find a way for the event to go ahead as planned.

Despite those efforts, the FIA said "ongoing uncertainty in the region and its effect on logistical arrangements" meant the WRC element of the event could not proceed.

The rally itself will still take place on the same dates as part of the FIA Middle East Rally Championship, with Saudi Arabia stressing it "remained ready to host the event safely and successfully" and that the Kingdom "continues to operate normally with national systems fully functional".

The WRC season will now instead conclude with the Sardinia Rally from October 1-4, becoming the 13th and final round of the year.

[Article continues below]

The F1 knock-on

The WRC calendar change comes just over two months before F1's own season finale swings through the Middle East, with Qatar's Lusail International Circuit hosting on November 29 and Abu Dhabi's Yas Marina Circuit closing out the campaign on December 6.

Addressing the WRC situation directly, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "We have worked closely with our partners in Saudi Arabia, our member club, the Saudi Automobile and Motorcycle Federation, WRC Promoter and our championship stakeholders in recent months to explore every possible route that would allow Rally Saudi Arabia to take place as planned.

"However, ongoing regional developments mean that the WRC element of Rally Saudi Arabia will not proceed this year. These are never easy decisions, particularly after the significant work undertaken by everyone involved in preparing for the event."

"While the WRC element of the event will not take place this year, our confidence in the organisers and in the long-term future of the rally remains unchanged.

"The FIA Middle East Rally Championship event will continue as planned in November, and we will continue to work closely with SAMF, SMC and the organising team to support the successful delivery of the event in November."

"Our focus now is firmly on the future. We will continue working together with our partners in Saudi Arabia and WRC Promoter towards bringing the FIA World Rally Championship back in 2027."

The calendar change still requires approval from the FIA World Motor Sport Council. F1's own calendar remains unaltered for now.

title: Lewis Hamilton issues stern statement to Ferrari shake-up rumours
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton must be seriously annoyed to come out with something so damning.

Lewis Hamilton has vehemently denied claims that he has asked Ferrari to replace members of his trackside crew.

It has been suggested by Italian publication Corriere della Sera that Hamilton is pushing team principal Frederic Vasseur to overhaul parts of his operational and strategy staff following friction during the European leg of the season.

The reports also point to a cooling relationship between Hamilton and Vasseur, with the Ferrari boss said to have rejected a post-Monza request from Hamilton for rigid written rules of engagement between him and team-mate Charles Leclerc.

Ferrari has undergone a series of engineering changes since the start of the year, with long-serving race engineer Riccardo Adami moved into a Driver Academy and historic testing role ahead of the 2026 campaign.

Luca Diella and Cedric Grosjean, arrivals from Mercedes and McLaren respectively, have since been integrated into Hamilton's crew, while the Scuderia has also added external chassis specialists over the summer to reinforce the technical department led by Loïc Serra.

Vasseur has previously dismissed talk of internal turmoil, framing driver requests for improvement as standard practice rather than evidence of a fractured relationship.

Ferrari has also defended Serra against external criticism, calling reports of leadership instability an unwanted distraction.

[Article continues below]

Driver

Hamilton sets the record straight

Hamilton has addressed the speculation directly on his Instagram page, rejecting any suggestion that he has called for personnel changes.

"I've seen some of the stories that have gone out, and I want to clear it up here," he wrote. "I've never asked for anyone on my team to be replaced.

"Everyone I work with works hard every day, and their dedication is what moves us forward.

"I always try to empower or lift people to be the best version of themselves, or at least see the best in themselves.

"I may not always achieve that, but it's my intention and what I'm here to do. We all work together, and that will continue."

No specific individuals within Ferrari's trackside operation were named in the original report.

title: Yuki Tsunoda highlights 'ego' as light shed on Red Bull struggles
excerpt:
Yuki Tsunoda has opened up on the struggles he endured with Red Bull following his promotion to the senior team in 2025.

Tsunoda was called up to replace Liam Lawson after the New Zealander endured a challenging opening two events with the Milton Keynes-based squad.

However, Tsunoda endured problems of his own and was frequently absent from the point-scoring positions throughout the year.

It led to his exit from the team at the end of 2025, with Isack Hadjar promoted in his place.

Tsunoda has acknowledged that he has a sizeable “ego” that left him reluctant to change his style behind the wheel.

“One thing about myself, I have big enough ego to not change my driving style,” Tsunoda told the Beyond The Grid podcast.

“I know what I'm doing in terms of driving and I believe in myself.

“I never try to change my driving style to other drivers, even though the driver is competitive and fast.”

[Article continues below]

Tsunoda: Driving style similar to Verstappen

Last year's finale in Abu Dhabi did not mark Tsunoda's final race in F1, as he was called up to Racing Bulls this year to replace Lawson, who stepped back up to Red Bull to replace an injured Hadjar.

His outings have been more competitive than those he endured at Red Bull alongside Verstappen.

But amid suggestions that the cars were developed to suit Verstappen in years gone by, Tsunoda found that his style behind the wheel resembled that of the four-time champion.

“Obviously for Max, it's a different case. He's a world champion, he proves a lot of things and I still learned a lot of things from his driving.

“My core driving is the same. And at some time, probably the first year out of any years since I started, I thought about changing driving style and trying to do something similar to Max.

“But in my perspective, if I just look at data, I didn't really see a huge difference in terms of driving.

“What I did most, and what I think now was the biggest mistake last year, was to try to replicate the set-up, what he's doing.

“Even knowing that sometimes, if I feel the car very oversteer, Max's[set-up] in theory makes the car worse, more sensitive in the direction change, or makes the car slide more.

“I tend to choose the set-up, even though I'm already struggling with oversteer. It can happen sometimes the opposite way as well.

“Even though I'm struggling with understeer, his car is more understeer. I try to replicate that.”

title: Williams rising star gains latest promotion
excerpt:
Williams Academy member Kean Nakamura-Berta will step up to F3 with Trident Motorsport next season, while continuing to receive backing from the Williams programme.

The 18-year-old joins Trident on the back of a strong FREC campaign, taking eight podiums, including three wins, to finish third overall.

Nakamura-Berta, who is half-Japanese and half-Slovakian, made his single-seater debut in the F4 South East Asia Championship in 2023 before finishing runner-up in the 2024 Formula 4 UAE Championship.

He enjoyed a breakout 2025, claiming back-to-back titles in the F4 Championship and Italian Formula 4, before adding the Formula Regional Middle East Trophy and third in FREC this year.

He follows 2025 F3 champion Rafael Câmara and runner-up Freddie Slater in making the same step from FREC to Trident.

[Article continues below]

F3 confidence boost

Nakamura-Berta said he was "pleased to be stepping up to F3" with the continued support of the Williams programme.

"Completing a strong season in FREC and having the opportunity to join such a competitive team in F3 gives me great confidence as I look ahead to my F3 debut next year. A big thank you to everyone involved who helped get me here."

Williams sporting director Sven Smeets called it "a proud moment to see Kean step up to F3 with Trident Motorsport for his rookie season," adding that it reflects "the opportunities it creates for the next generation of talented drivers."

title: Ferrari driver intervention shut down: 'Not an option for them'
excerpt:
Former F1 driver David Coulthard believes Ferrari has no scope to inflict driver status on Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc within the team.

Hamilton joined the Italian squad last year from Mercedes, with the sport's most successful driver linking up with the most triumphant team.

He partnered up with Leclerc, who has been part of the Maranello-based squad since 2019 after spending several years in its junior programme.

While Leclerc was the better performer in 2025, Hamilton has stepped up his game this year and currently leads his team-mate in the standings.

However, their working relationship came into question earlier this month at the Italian Grand Prix, when Leclerc seemed to push Hamilton wide and into the gravel on the opening lap.

It resulted in some comments that Ferrari should have implemented a number one driver status within the team in a bid to chase down Mercedes and Kimi Antonelli - but Coulthard stated such a possibility is non-existent between two high-calibre drivers.

“I don't think it is an option for them,” Coulthard told the Up to Speed podcast.

“You employ Lewis Hamilton, and you've got Charles Leclerc, who's been there for several years, is blindingly fast and a sort of poster boy for a racing driver.

“Good-looking, he's got the family, a baby on the way, a dog in the paddock... my opinion is that's all a bit too much, quite frankly.

“It's not a weekend away picnic, is it? It's a grand prix, it's a serious business. It's a dangerous business, but that's probably me being of an older generation.

“They [Ferrari] don't have a choice. They've employed two of the best drivers in the world.

“You then manage them as best you can.”

[Article continues below]

Coulthard suspects Ferrari rules of engagement already exist

Hamilton insisted after the Monza race that the approach to working together to cut into Mercedes' lead was now too late.

Both drivers played down the significance of the incident on the opening lap, which marked the biggest flashpoint yet between the two Ferrari drivers.

When asked if Ferrari should introduce rules of engagement, Coulthard replied: “I suspect they do.

“There'll be somewhere in the contract that says that the driver has to take fair and reasonable instructions from a senior member of the team.

“That's a pretty generic clause that's in all contracts because otherwise you could employ a driver and he could go rogue.

“You couldn't fire him because you don't have a clause that says, 'look, you're really not behaving yourself'.”

title: Max Verstappen 'acted on instinct' to survive 100 karters 'chaos'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has explained how he acted "on instinct" to survive the "chaos" of the opening laps of Max vs 100 at Silverstone.

On Wednesday, the four-time F1 drivers' champion started 101st in a special Red Bull event at the home of the British GP - and 35 minutes later, had passed all 100 to pull off the win.

At the start, chaos erupted at Turn 1 with the field all bunching up as Verstappen was forced to take to the run-off before slowly picking off the runners to leave himself with three drivers to go, including a Dutch F1 journalist Jacky Martens and a member of his Red Bull team, Louis Osler.

After some bumper cars, Verstappen emerged victorious, and spoke of how respectful the 100 karters had been towards him.

"You just act on instinct to whatever happens, right?" Verstappen explained to invited media, including RacingNews365.

"When the lights go out, you just see where the gaps are, and then you also need to trust a few people around you that they don't do anything crazy, and I mean, to be honest, they didn't.

"They were very excited with each other, but they were actually quite nice to me, to not, like, crash to me or whatever. But you just act really quickly when you just see everything unfold in front of you.

"The first half [of the race] is just chaos, so you just want to survive, and then after that, you're just hunting them down.

"So it is quite nice where you just have to put the laps in yourself and catch them one-by-one.

"At one point, I said before the race, 'let's be bold and say that I would pass 40 people on Lap 1,' and then they told me it was 61 I think.

"So it was a good effort, and I just had to stay out of trouble. Some people got really excited and there was a bit of a roadblock going on, but I managed to swerve around it."

The article continues below.

Verstappen pulls off 100 karters challenge

When then asked by RacingNews365 what he thought was realistic coming into the race and if he believed the win was possible, Verstappen indicated that he felt it was all along.

"Well, I knew my lap times when I did the prep laps, and I knew the qualifying lap times of the others, so I knew the win was possible," he said.

"But it really depended on my first two laps, and they went better than expected, so that helped a lot."

title: Lando Norris pinpoints 'never before' challenge for new Monaco F1 Sprint
excerpt:
Lando Norris has identified what he believes will be the big challenge at the 2027 Monaco Grand Prix, which will be a Sprint race.

As the 2027 calendar was unveiled on Wednesday, it was confirmed that Monaco would be one of 10 Sprint events next season.

The rationale behind this is that it will give the grand prix two qualifying sessions, usually the highlight of the weekend.

Another factor is that heading into Sprint Qualifying, drivers will only have one 60-minute practice session, as opposed to the usual three before the grid is set in the Principality.

This challenge is something that immediately struck 2025 Monaco winner Norris.

"Interesting, interesting," Norris told Sky Sports F1.

"I guess the main thing is that means we've got FP1 and qualifying on Friday, which is the challenge, and obviously, not a lot happens in a race on Sunday, or in the Sprint.

"But I think the challenge is just one practice session and straight in [to qualifying], which I think has probably never happened before in Monaco."

The article continues below.

Risk vs reward

Knowing how to balance the risk vs reward in Monaco qualifying is hihglighted as one of the best examples of driver skill, as Norris explained how some are prepared to be "comfy" and not go the extra mile.

"We'll be relying more on data from this year, and obviously, it is tougher for us as drivers," Norris added.

"You don't have much time to build up to things, so you're probably going to have to try and risk a little bit more earlier, which is when you can see a bit more of a difference between people who can get comfy, try things, and be at 99% and not go 103-104%, because in Monaco, when you go to that limit, it's game over."
